                                  SAVE THE LAMPASAS’ REPLY BRIEF
            Pursuant to State Office of Administrative Hearings (SOAH) Order Nos. 6 and 32, Save

   the Lampasas1 timely files this Reply Brief on June 26, 2026 and if the Honorable Administrative

   Law Judges (ALJs) and the Public Utility Commission of Texas (Commission or PUC) find that

   the project meets the statutory criteria, that they only do so with approval a route that avoids

   fragmentation across the Lampasas River Valley and crosses the Colorado River at the

   southernmost proposed crossing, such as Route 296 or Route 572 above other routes available in

   this proceeding.


                                              I.    INTRODUCTION

           On June 19, 2026, the parties in this proceeding, including Save the Lampasas, filed initial

   briefs under SOAH Order Nos. 6 and 32. Save the Lampasas responds to initial briefs advocating

   that the Commission select Route 894, as well as initial briefs advocating for routes that support




           1
             Save the Lampasas is an aligned group of intervenors representing more than 50 noticed affected property
   owners and over 550 interested members of the community participating as Save the Lampasas 25, Inc.




                                                                                                                        003
                                                                                          Page 3 of 24


routes that unduly fragment the Lampasas River Valley’s watershed and/or would cross the

Colorado River at a previously undisturbed area.

       Overall, Save the Lampasas continues to oppose Route 894, and appreciates the Applicants

acknowledgment that there are many routes in the Routes of Interest (including Routes 296 and/or

572) which they can support. As demonstrated here, the evidence when considered as a whole

demonstrates that Route 894, including Links G51 and G52, does not comply with the applicable

statutory and regulatory routing criteria by bisecting an inordinate number of properties through

previously undisturbed sensitive portions of the Study Area, crossing the Colorado River at a

previously undisturbed portion of the river to the detriment of Texas Parks and Wildlife

Department (TPWD) Colorado Bend State Park and Post Oak Ridge State Park and the users of

those parks, unnecessarily negatively impacts the Lampasas River Valley, and implicates

unaddressed engineering constraints, among other concerns. Rather, it is Save the Lampasas’s

position that both Route 296 and Route 572, or instead, a combination of Routes 296 and 572, best

address the routing criteria and best protect the Texas Hill Country regions in this study area from

being forever and irreparably changed by this project.


                               II.   NEED FOR THE PROJECT

        This case could unleash permanent and irreversible impacts on areas of Texas that have

and will remain protected and preserved in the hands of many generations of Texas families.

Before that were to happen, the Commission must be sure that it has carefully considered

reasonable means to avail itself of all available information and policy considerations to determine

whether that level of permanent alteration of Texas Hill Country communities is warranted. For

example, decisions around the implementation of Senate Bill 6 could significantly change the

planning criteria used to support this project. Further, new generation announcements closer to




                                                                                                        004
                                                                                                       Page 4 of 24


the Permian Basin could significantly alter the required transfer capability. In addition, for this

particular project, reason must prevail in carefully considering the fact that there are no new

generation announcements identified by the Applicants that would support a conclusion that this

particular proposed project would be connected to generation sources capable of injecting power

to be imported.

           The Applicants’ Initial Brief contains generalized conclusory statements that are

insufficient to meet their burden of proof to establish the statutory factor of need for this project.

The Applicants rely heavily on legislation passed in 2023 to attempt to assert need in this case,

stating:

           “These projects satisfy H.B. 5066’s directive to increase capacity to meet forecasted load.”2

           Unlike the build-out of transmission associated with the Competitive Renewable Energy

Zones, H.B. 5066 did not find that inclusion in the Permian Basin Reliability Plan constitutes a

legislative determination of need. The entirety of the legislation that required the Commission to

issue the Permian Basis Reliability Plan in H.B. 5066 (which expired on its own terms on

September 1, 2025) and states:

           Sec. 39.167. RELIABILITY PLAN FOR PERMIAN BASIN. (Added by HB 5066)

                   (a) Not later than January 30, 2024, the commission shall direct the
           independent organization certified under Section 39.151 for the ERCOT power
           region to develop a reliability plan under Section 39.166 for the Permian Basin
           region.

       Nor did the Commission make a determination in the Order approving the Permian Basin

Reliability Plan that the Permian Basin Plan created a presumption of need. The Preliminary Order

in this case requires the Applicant to address all of the essential elements for a determination of

need. Mr. Gurley’s conclusory statements and reliance on the Permian Basin Reliability Plan do

not satisfy the burden of proof in this case.3 Further, even if the ALJs determined that the Permian

Basis Reliability Plan was sufficient to support a finding of need in this case, the PBRP supports

only a determination that this project may be needed in 2038. The Commission Order approving

the PRBP required ERCOT to work with the TSPs to identify the import paths that would be

needed to serve load in 2030 to prioritize those CCN applications. Accordingly, at most, this case

should not proceed at haste.

       Applicants rely on the testimony of Mr. Gurley and the ERCOT Permian Basis Reliability

Plan he attached to his testimony, but none of this analysis provides information that the project

contained in the pending Application is incrementally necessary to serve the Permian Basin load

that was underlying that Application.4

         ERCOT’s forecast shows an exponential increase in the number of non-oil and gas loads

in the Permian Basin.5 Furthermore, the Commission is still in the process of setting standards for

how much those prospective new loads will actually contribute to peak load on the system, given

mandatory offsets for on-site generation or controllable load. In fact, the Commission has sent

ERCOT back to rework its load forecasts using the freshly adopted Batch Zero process to inform

that analysis.6


                                       III.     ROUTE ADEQUACY

         While the Commission allowed the order to stand that found that the application contains

an adequate number of routes, that order does not determine whether any of the routes comply

with the applicable statutory and regulatory routing criteria. The Commission should be aware of

long-standing Commission precedent in this very study area that ultimately determined that the

Application should be denied if the only viable option involved crossing the Colorado River in the

same area of the Colorado River as is proposed by parties supporting Route 894.


                                       IV.     ROUTING CRITERIA


                     1.    Community Values

Riparian impacts

         A recurring topic in the parties’ initial briefs is the impacts on riparian areas. Many argue

that the riparian impacts are the most distinguishing aspect of the various alternative routes.7

        Those parties supporting Route 894 place less emphasis on discussion of riparian impacts

because, Route 894 performs very poorly when considering riparian impacts and their importance

to the consideration of community values, parks and recreational areas, the environment, and

aesthetic impacts. All alternative routes in the study area cross the Colorado River and the San

Saba River. The Commission has recognized concerns about impacts on major rivers and their

associated watersheds that run through the Texas Hill Country within the study area.8 In Docket

No. 37463, the Commission based its routing decision in part on selecting a route that avoided

impacts to the Lampasas River’s watershed and its tributaries. Further, crossings of the Colorado

River and impacts to the neighboring State Park of Colorado Bend State Park (now joined by the

adjacent Post Oak Ridge State Park on the east side of the river) have been pivotal in Commission

precedent.9 Replies to Initial Briefs in the context of these riparian impacts are presented here,

moving from East to West in the study area.

Lampasas River Watershed

        Tellingly, no party offered any briefing attempting to assert the benefits of Links G51 and

G52 in Route 894. These segments directly affect the Lampasas River Watershed, including

Panther Creek, Mesquite Creek, Burnet Branch, Panther Den Branch, Miller Creek, and Mill

Creek, impacts that have been disfavored by the Commission and comments of TPWD in the

past.10 Initial Briefs supporting Route 894 are silent with regard to the clear evidence that Links

G51 and G52 would have severe impacts on the entire Lampasas River Watershed area, especially

Rocky Creek (which has been designated as an Ecologically Sensitive Stream), Mesquite Creek,

and Panther Creek, which are crossed or closely paralleled multiple times.11 The Lampasas River

Watershed is an undisturbed riparian area for which fragmentation should be avoided.12 Many

initial briefs describe the impact to individual properties by portions of links that bisect their

properties. However, those same concerns apply to essentially every property on links G51, G52,

and U1 that are members of Save the Lampasas. Referencing a simple counting of habitable

structures within the notice corridor does not allow proper balancing of the impacts to an entire

community.

Colorado River

       No party offers evidence to show that Colorado River Crossings presented in the

Application at J22 (or J26) perform the best when considering any of the statutory factors of

community values, parks and recreational areas, environment, and aesthetics. Nor does any party

challenge the substance of the evidence from TPWD, which objects to crossing at J22 because it

is in the viewshed of both Colorado Bend State Park and Post Oak Ridge State Park.

       The parties advocating for crossing the Colorado River at J22 do so as part of their support

for Route 894, relying heavily on the fact that it appears to perform well mathematically on the

Tables, with estimated costs and habitable structures in the low range among the routes presented

in the application.13 These aspects are discussed in the relevant portions of this Reply Brief.

         In their Initial Briefs, both the Brady Creek Intervenors and the Solana Intervenors state

that Link J31 “would introduce new transmission infrastructure into undeveloped portions of the

Colorado River environment.”14 This statement is contrary to the record evidence that a long-

standing corridor of multiple pipelines crosses the Colorado River near the Segment J31 River

crossing. This infrastructure corridor was disturbed by multiple pipeline installations as recently

as 2017 and has been the subject of a prior proposed routing from LCRA in PUC Docket No.

37448.15 Link J31 should be used for crossing the Colorado River, as it parallels an existing

previously disturbed corridor and is consistent with the ALJs’ decission and Commission precedent

that found this crossing to be better than a proposed crossing in closer proximity to the Colorado

Bend State Park area.16 From an environmental perspective, it is preferable to co-locate new

infrastructure parallel to or in close proximity to existing infrastructure corridors where land has

been recently disturbed, rather than in previously undisturbed areas.17 In fact, the Brady Creek

Intervenors’ and Solana Intervenors’ briefs correctly observe that Link J22 is previously

undisturbed at the Colorado River Crossing, and is unacceptably close to Colorado Bend State

Park and Post Oak Ridge State Park.18

                   2.       Engineering Constraints – Airports and Helipads

        Initial Briefs supporting Route 894 do not address the constraints related to airports and

helipads by intersecting an FAA-registered airport and a helipad, significant issues that both Routes

296 and 572 avoid.

         Neither initial briefs supporting Route 894, nor the Applicants’ Initial Brief offer any

specific solution for addressing the Salado Bluffs Airport, which is intersected by Route 894 at

Links E52 and F1.22 Similarly, the Initial Briefs supporting Route 894 do not offer any specific

solution for elimination of the conflict with FAA regulations that would be present for the FAA

registered Windy Ridge Airport, which is completely bisected by Link U1. As demonstrated in

the evidence, an airport intersection by a link is a severe and unusual characteristic of an initially

proposed transmission line, let alone of a route designated as the best-meets route by an applicant,

with Mr. Marusak conceding that he could not recall a previous instance of an airport intersection

being identified in an initial application.23 Mr. Marusak then explained that the Applicant's

awareness of the Salado Bluffs Airport “came very, very late [in the application preparation

process]” and that, had they been aware of its existence beforehand, they would have “analyzed

the links differently.” 24

Route 296 - School Issue Should Not Be Determinative

         Multiple intervenors point to the proposed location of Link F34 within the notice distance

to the Florence Independent School District’s (FISD) new school as a claimed means to disqualify

Route 296.54

         The fact that a portion of a transmission line may be sited near a school is not, in and of

itself, disqualifying. Rather, it is one data point that must be analyzed holistically with the rest of

a proposed project’s attributes. In Application of the City of San Antonio, Acting by and Through

the City Public Service Board (CPS Energy), to Amend its Certificate of Convenience and

Necessity for the Omicron 138-KV Transmission Line in Bexar County, the Commission approved

a transmission line that would come within 500 feet of a school.55 In Omicron, the ALJ stated that

the utility has been operating transmission facilities with ROW on school properties, and that

school districts have developed properties in the utility’s service area adjacent to existing

transmission facilities.56 The ALJ further stated that no special weight is given to schools when

applying the Commission's prudent avoidance policy.57 Commission Staff also questioned the

                             V.    SUMMARY AND CONCLUSION

                             V.    SUMMARY AND CONCLUSION

       No party has provided sufficient evidence demonstrating that a route that decimates

undisturbed riparian areas ofthe Texas Hill Country, which the communities and the State, through

the parks system, have held dear for generations, is warranted. Accordingly, if the Commission

determines that the overall public necessity for this line warrants approval of a route at this time,

the record evidence most supports selecting a route that uses the southern corridor to cross the

Colorado River and reduce the impacts to the Lampasas River Valley, such as Route 296 or Route

572. It is critical to note that as to the portion of the project in Williamson and Bell Counties, any

routing preference of the ALJs and the Commission can accommodate this routing imperative -

that is, to avoid destruction and fragmentation of currently undisturbed riparian corridors

associated with the watersheds of the Colorado River and the Lampasas River. Accordingly, any

ofthe Routes of Interest in Williamson and Bell counties can be followed, then connect to the links

that make up Routes 296 or 572 beginning at Link G6.


       The ALJs and the Commission are assisted by and should rely on prior PUC precedent

specific to Burnet County in this study area. This precedent supports protecting these undisturbed

riparian areas of the Lampasas River Valley and supports a finding that the Southern crossing of

the Colorado River along the existing fragmented pipeline corridor at Link J31 better complies

with the applicable routing criteria than a crossing within less than a mile of the Colorado Bend

and Post Oak Ridge State Parks.


       Save the Lampasas appreciates the extensive efforts undertaken by the ALJs and the

Commission and respectfully requests that, if a route is approved as meeting the standards for

public convenience and necessity, it follow either Route 296 or Route 572 in Burnet County and

the counties to the west, no matter which route is selected in Bell and Williamson Counties.
